source.excerpt: Fix reason firmly in her seat, and call to her tribunal every fact, every opinion. Question with boldness even the existence of a god; because, if there be one, he must more approve the homage of reason, than that of blindfolded fear.
trail: The quote is the words of Thomas Jefferson, from his 10 August 1787 letter to his nephew Peter Carr, transcribed on Monticello’s Jefferson Quotes & Family Letters ↗.
The full letter, including the “Fix reason firmly in her seat” passage, appears in Founders Online ↗ (National Archives) and the Letters of Thomas Jefferson ↗.
Jefferson advises Carr to examine religion by reason without fear of its consequences; the sentence sits inside a longer counsel on study, corroborated at Encyclopedia Virginia ↗.
source.excerptNote: Jefferson’s manuscript uses lowercase “god” and the reading “approve the homage”; some later transcriptions modernize the capital and insert “of.”

author.bio: Thomas Jefferson drafted the Declaration of Independence, served as first U.S. Secretary of State and third president, and founded the University of Virginia. Writing from Paris in 1787, he sent his young nephew Peter Carr a celebrated letter of study advice whose religion section urged reason over inherited fear. The passage became a touchstone of his reputation as an Enlightenment rationalist.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Jefferson wrote from Paris to his teenage nephew, Peter Carr, laying out a full course of study. The section on religion is the letter’s most quoted: rather than warn Carr away from doubt, Jefferson tells him to interrogate every claim — even God’s existence — at “the tribunal” of reason.
The line has since become a banner for Enlightenment rationalism and church–state separation, and it is genuinely Jefferson’s own words rather than a later paraphrase.
